items.title: How DARPA Challenged Teams to Bring Robots Into Disaster Triage
items.summary: On 5 November, 10 teams descended upon a 52-acre mock town in College Station, Texas called Disaster City. They were there for a nine-day competition to see how well teams of robots and humans could navigate simulated catastrophes, like a market ravaged by a tornado and a nighttime strike on a military base. At stake? US $2.5 million in prize money.The scenarios were the final of the DARPA Triage Challenge, which the U.S. agency has been running for three years with the goal of saving more lives in urgent mass casualty events. Engineers from academia and industry have competed in elaborately staged mass casualty events, such as simulated combat zones and plane crash scenes. Teams spent years designing systems where autonomous ground robots and drones could help first responders find mock victims and decide the best way to care for them. “Triage is all about resources,” says Jeremy Pamplin, who managed the challenge for DARPA. Pamplin is a critical care physician and retired colonel who spent 28 years in the U.S. Army.In mass casualty events, medics race to assess trauma with finite resources and limited time. Some victims need urgent help that medics can provide immediately, like tourniquets to halt bleeding. Some need evacuation and surgery. Others don’t need immediate help—either because their wounds are minimal enough, or because they’re so severe that a medic’s attention is better served elsewhere. Medics must prioritize who gets what care, but the line between each of these scenarios can be murky amid the rubble, frenzy, and heat of the moment.It’s a difficult problem, and so the technologies developed in this competition could help real-world decisionmaking, says Gabriela Garcia Dolagaray, assistant medical director for emergency preparedness at Massachusetts General Hospital and the Brigham and Women’s Hospital in Boston. “Finding people can sometimes just be dangerous,” she says, “and getting a robust number of people to go out and search in a disaster area will take time.”Trauma Technologies and the DARPA Triage ChallengeThe Triage Challenge is the latest in a long DARPA legacy of running grand challenges to incentivize proof-of-concept development of important technologies. This particular challenge began as a program to quickly detect signs of trauma. DARPA imagined not only that drones and robots could find casualties, but that machine learning algorithms could assist in triage—which, at its core, is the process of assessing injuries and prioritizing care in a medical emergency.Pamplin took over the competition in May 2025. “I have friends that still wake up in the middle of the night with these types of recollections and wondering if they did the right thing in the moment during a mass casualty incident,” Pamplin says. “That moves me. I would very much like to eliminate that uncertainty for them to the extent possible with this type of technology.”He used his experience to make the competition increasingly elaborate and realistic. Year one featured a simulated convoy attack, and human participants sat in protective enclosures to avoid incidental run-ins with robots. In year two, when Pamplin took over the challenge, his team incorporated a full-size airplane fuselage to simulate a plane crash with dozens of victims. Organizers learned to recreate the physical environment of a disaster, and also the physical signs of injuries, like warm blood. Pamplin’s team visited a slaughterhouse with thermal cameras to study the temperature of blood spilling onto the ground. In the competition, they mimic that effect by heating water in a coffee pot and pouring it beside the body. This lets teams detect bleeding even at night.  A man performs a simulated triage as part of DARPA’s Triage Challenge finals. The program was designed to see how robots could assist in making triage decisions during an emergency.Paul Flacks/DARPA“They always are throwing additional challenging things at us that you wouldn’t expect,” says Sam Colachis, a biomedical engineer at Battelle, an applied science and technology nonprofit in Columbus Ohio who led the organization’s DART team—short for “Drone-Assisted Rapid Triage”—in the competition.The tactics required for successful triage are inherently multidisciplinary, says Derek Paley, a professor of aerospace engineering leading the University of Maryland’s team, RoboScout. Before 2022, Paley felt confident in his lab’s skills with autonomous navigation and algorithms, but he knew little about trauma medicine. “I didn’t even know what triage was,” he says. Paley recruited colleagues in emergency medicine to help design his team’s approach and shape their tech. Before the Triage Challenge began, they felt like an underdog. “We kind of have a chip on our shoulder because we think we can play on the same field as these other teams…who’ve done grand challenges before,” Paley told Spectrum before the competition. They finished third in the first year of competition and second last year.Ea
